# Summary of 2024 General Election Manifesto

This manifesto addresses what it identifies as interconnected crises: cost of living pressures, climate emergency, and declining public services. It argues that solutions to environmental challenges simultaneously address economic inequality and service provision.

## Healthcare and Social Care

The document proposes significant NHS investment, including £28bn additional annual expenditure by 2030 and £20bn capital spending over five years. Key commitments include reducing waiting lists, guaranteeing GP access, ensuring universal NHS dentistry access, boosting staff pay, and restoring public health budgets. It opposes NHS privatisation and supports the NHS Reinstatement Bill.

For social care, it advocates free personal care, increased carer pay with career structures, and £20bn annual investment. Disability benefits would increase by 5%, with opposition to replacing cash payments with vouchers.

## Housing

The manifesto proposes 150,000 new social homes annually, ending right-to-buy, empowering local authorities to introduce rent controls, and ending no-fault evictions. A major retrofit programme would invest £29bn over five years to insulate homes, with additional funding for heating systems and climate adaptation.

## Energy and Environment

Energy proposals include achieving 70% wind-generated electricity by 2030, ending new fossil fuel licences and subsidies, promoting community energy ownership, and opposing nuclear power. A carbon tax starting at £120 per tonne would rise to £500 within ten years.

Environmental commitments include a Rights of Nature Act, protecting 30% of land and seas by 2030, returning water companies to public ownership, and strengthening pollution enforcement.

## Economy and Taxation

The manifesto proposes £40bn average annual green investment, bringing railways, water companies, and major energy retailers into public ownership. Tax reforms include a wealth tax on assets above £10m, aligning capital gains with income tax rates, and removing the upper earnings limit on National Insurance. Business taxes would increase, particularly windfall taxes on oil, gas, and banking profits.

## Work and Welfare

Proposals include a £15 minimum wage regardless of age, maximum 10:1 pay ratios, repealing anti-union legislation, and moving toward a four-day working week. Universal Credit would increase by £40 weekly, the two-child benefit cap would be abolished, and the five-week benefit wait would end.

## Education

Education commitments include £8bn school investment, £2bn teacher pay uplift, addressing unsafe buildings, free school meals for all children, abolishing tuition fees, restoring maintenance grants, and eventually cancelling graduate debt. Special needs provision would receive £5bn investment.

## Transport

Transport proposals include £10bn annual public transport subsidies, railway renationalisation, local authority bus control, £2.5bn annual cycling and walking investment, and ending petrol and diesel vehicle sales by 2027. Aviation measures include a frequent-flyer levy and banning short domestic flights.

## Democracy and Rights

Democratic reforms include proportional representation, votes at 16, replacing the House of Lords with an elected chamber, and repealing voter ID requirements. The manifesto defends the Human Rights Act and European Convention on Human Rights, opposes recent protest restrictions, and supports trans self-identification.

## Immigration

Immigration proposals include ending the hostile environment, creating safe asylum routes, permitting asylum seekers to work during applications, ending immigration detention except for public safety, and removing minimum income requirements for family visas.

## International Affairs

International commitments include supporting Ukraine, calling for an immediate bilateral ceasefire between Israel and Gaza, recognising Palestine, ending UK arms exports to Israel, increasing overseas aid to 1% of GNI, and working toward EU membership. The manifesto supports signing the UN Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons and cancelling the Trident programme, while acknowledging NATO's security role but advocating reforms including no-first-use nuclear policies.
